newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa faces crisis as weak gold hits miners.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa faces crisis as weak gold hits miners.

text.p: South Africa is facing its worst social crisis with sliding gold prices threatening a surge in unemployment, analysts said.
More than 50,000 miners could lose their jobs if gold prices fail below its current 12-year low.
"It could be the worst thing the country has ever seen. This gold crisis is the last thing the country needs right now," an analyst said.
But it is not just miners, mostly black and earning around 2,000 rand a month ($444), who are threatened by poverty.
Many of South Africa's gold mines are the only source of income for many small towns, which could become ghost towns.
"It will have a catastrophic effect. All these towns would become sleepy pension villages," said Grahame Graham-Parker, general manager of Infinity Asset Management.
Gold prices have fallen to the lowest since 1985, pinching an already squeezed industry.
Among the producers with the highest costs in the world due to the nature of the deep, labour-intensive mines, South African gold mines have suffered falling output since the 1970s.
Production in 1970 was just more than 1,000 tonnes. Last year, 496 tonnes were produced. This year looks little brighter with 500 tonnes expected.
The gold industry has already cut mine jobs from around 530,000 in 1987 to around 350,000 in 1996.
With a gold price around $320 an ounce, more mines are flung into the marginal camp and more jobs are on the line as producers seek to cut costs further to guarantee profitability.

Roger Baxter, chief economist at the employer body Chamber of Mines, said that in the first three months of 1997 nine gold mines employing 63,000 people were classified as marginal and seven of those were operating at a loss.
Newspaper reports put the number of mine jobs currently under threat at 100,000. Baxter declined to give a number while analysts say the number is likely to be more than 50,000.

With a third of the country's population of around 38 million out of work, any job cuts would severely burden President Nelson Mandela's government, which has been struggling to deliver jobs since it was elected in April 1994.
The National Union of Mineworkers (NUM), seeking to soften the blow through talks with mine management, says the crisis might have been avoided if employers had met labour half-way years ago.

"But...the industry didn't have a social responsibility in terms of downsizing," said Ben Molapo, NUM spokesman."For years, we have been negotiating with them. But from both the government and the industry we never got a concrete response."
Some analysts said the crisis has been compounded by the industry's "apartheid mentality."

"It's no secret South African mines are the largest employer in this country. The miners have been very, very badly treated. The NUM has often come to the party (annual wage negotiations) with increase demands well below inflation," said Graham-Parker."They (the NUM) came as brokers and did not hold a gun to the industry's head. On many occasions, they took less than inflationary increases and were rewarded by job cuts."
But producers and other analysts said labour action like strikes have hit already falling productivity.

The chamber and the NUM are embroiled in annual wage talks. The NUM is seeking a minimum wage of 1,800 rand ($400) a month for underground workers. The industry is finding ways of increasing productivity by working more shifts.
